The rocket that Kofi and Ray built for the egg-loft event at the Millard County Rocketry Club stood a little taller than Kofi's arm, and Kofi had designed nearly all of it. He had chosen the fins, worked out where the weight should sit, and carved the foam cradle that would hold one raw egg inside the clear plastic capsule that formed the rocket's nose. Ray had been given what was left: packing the parachute.

Kofi thought that was the easy part. Ray did not seem to agree. On the Thursday before the launch, Kofi watched him lay the orange parachute flat on the club table, fold it in thirds, then in thirds again, and wind the lines around the bundle in a loose spiral. Twice he shook it out and started over. Then he dusted the folds with baby powder from a little bottle he had brought from home.

"It's plastic," Ray said, when Kofi asked. "Folded tight, it sticks to itself. The powder keeps it from sticking."

Last came the wadding, three squares of flame-resistant paper pushed down the tube first, so that they sat between the motor and the parachute. A few seconds after the motor burned out, a small charge would fire upward to pop off the nose and push the parachute free. The wadding was there so that the hot gas would reach the paper first and the parachute second.

On Saturday the field smelled of cut hay. Mrs. Ostrowski ran the launches from a folding table, and she did not hand anyone the safety key until the pad was clear. Kofi carried the rocket out, slid it onto the launch rail, and walked back to the line. Someone counted down from five.

The rocket went up with a hiss and a thin trail of smoke, straight as a pencil. At the top of its climb there was a soft pop, the nose swung loose on its cord, and the orange parachute opened all at once. It drifted down over the hay and set the rocket in the grass so gently that it barely tipped.

Kofi ran. He unscrewed the capsule with shaking fingers and held up the egg, whole, and the club cheered. Mrs. Ostrowski wrote Kofi's name on the board under EGG LOFT: SUCCESSFUL.

Later, when the others had gone back to their own rockets, Kofi looked around for Ray. He found him sitting in the grass by the launch rail with the parachute spread across his knees, picking bits of hay out of the lines one at a time.

Kofi sat down next to him. After a minute he said, "Show me how you fold it."

At the back of the Lindqvist pasture, where the cows
stopped grazing before I was born, an oak stands
by itself, with a strand of wire that enters its trunk
on one side and comes out again on the other.

Someone stapled that wire to it when the tree
was thin enough to circle with two hands,
a post already planted, needing nothing,
and ran the pasture's edge from it, and went home.

The tree went on with the one work it knows,
laying down a ring of wood each summer
around the staple first, and then the wire,
the bark rolling slowly over both

the way slow water covers a dropped stone.
The posts on either side have rotted down.
The rest of the fence lies coiled in the grass,
its barbs rusted as blunt as burrs.

But here, five feet up, the wire still runs
straight and tight into the wood, and out,
held fast by the thing it was meant to use.
I lay my hand on the swelling there,

the bark ridged up around the metal
like the seam of a healed cut, and think
how long it takes to grow around a thing,
a ring a year, each one too thin to notice,

and how whoever strung this line
meant the oak to work for the fence.
It is the fence that has lasted by the oak:
the last few feet of it still standing

stand inside a tree that kept on growing
and took the wire in, and did not let it go.

stopped grazing before I was born, an oak stands
by itself, with a strand of wire that enters its trunk
on one side and comes out again on the other.

Someone stapled that wire to it when the tree
was thin enough to circle with two hands,
a post already planted, needing nothing,
and ran the pasture's edge from it, and went home.

The tree went on with the one work it knows,
laying down a ring of wood each summer
around the staple first, and then the wire,
the bark rolling slowly over both

the way slow water covers a dropped stone.
The posts on either side have rotted down.
The rest of the fence lies coiled in the grass,
its barbs rusted as blunt as burrs.

But here, five feet up, the wire still runs
straight and tight into the wood, and out,
held fast by the thing it was meant to use.
I lay my hand on the swelling there,

the bark ridged up around the metal
like the seam of a healed cut, and think
how long it takes to grow around a thing,
a ring a year, each one too thin to notice,

and how whoever strung this line
meant the oak to work for the fence.
It is the fence that has lasted by the oak:
the last few feet of it still standing

stand inside a tree that kept on growing
and took the wire in, and did not let it go.

Every Saturday in summer my mother hung the sheets on the line behind our house, and every Saturday afternoon my sister Maren and I were sent out to bring them in. She was fourteen and I was eleven, and that year we could hardly pass each other in the hallway without an argument.

A hand towel can be folded by one person. A sheet for a double bed has to be folded by two. We would each take two corners of one end and back away from each other until the sheet hung between us, then lift it and snap it once, hard, so that it flattened in the air. Next each of us brought our own two corners together, and the sheet was half as wide. Then came the part we both hated. One of us had to walk forward, all the way up to the other, and hand over the corners, and the other had to take them.

For most of that summer the walking forward was the whole argument. Maren said it was my turn. I said I had done it last week. We stood at opposite ends of the yard with the sheet sagging into the grass between us, each waiting for the other to move, until our mother leaned out of the kitchen window and called that the sheets would be dirty again before they were folded.

Then one of us would go. Usually it was Maren, because she was older and could pretend she was doing it only to get the job finished. She would walk up to me with the corners held out at arm's length, and I would take them without looking at her, and she would bend for the bottom fold, and we would back away again and do it once more, smaller.

Something happened in that walk that I understood only later. You cannot hand someone the corners of a sheet from across a yard. You have to come close enough to touch their hands, and once you are that close, it is hard to keep up whatever you had been saying.

By August we had stopped arguing about whose turn it was. I could not tell you when it stopped. We simply began meeting in the middle, both stepping forward at once, so that each of us walked only half the way.

Maren lives in an apartment in the city now, and her dryer has a setting for everything. When I visit, though, she still pulls a clean sheet out of the basket, holds two corners out toward me, and waits.

Every Saturday in summer my mother hung the sheets on the line behind our house, and every Saturday afternoon my sister Maren and I were sent out to bring them in. She was fourteen and I was eleven, and that year we could hardly pass each other in the hallway without an argument.

A hand towel can be folded by one person. A sheet for a double bed has to be folded by two. We would each take two corners of one end and back away from each other until the sheet hung between us, then lift it and snap it once, hard, so that it flattened in the air. Next each of us brought our own two corners together, and the sheet was half as wide. Then came the part we both hated. One of us had to walk forward, all the way up to the other, and hand over the corners, and the other had to take them.

For most of that summer the walking forward was the whole argument. Maren said it was my turn. I said I had done it last week. We stood at opposite ends of the yard with the sheet sagging into the grass between us, each waiting for the other to move, until our mother leaned out of the kitchen window and called that the sheets would be dirty again before they were folded.

Then one of us would go. Usually it was Maren, because she was older and could pretend she was doing it only to get the job finished. She would walk up to me with the corners held out at arm's length, and I would take them without looking at her, and she would bend for the bottom fold, and we would back away again and do it once more, smaller.

Something happened in that walk that I understood only later. You cannot hand someone the corners of a sheet from across a yard. You have to come close enough to touch their hands, and once you are that close, it is hard to keep up whatever you had been saying.

By August we had stopped arguing about whose turn it was. I could not tell you when it stopped. We simply began meeting in the middle, both stepping forward at once, so that each of us walked only half the way.

Maren lives in an apartment in the city now, and her dryer has a setting for everything. When I visit, though, she still pulls a clean sheet out of the basket, holds two corners out toward me, and waits.

When I finish writing something, an essay or a long letter or a report for work, I put it in a drawer. Sometimes the drawer is real, and sometimes it is only a folder on my computer that I promise myself to leave closed. Either way, the piece stays there for at least three days before I read it again. Of everything I have learned about writing, this is the habit I would pass on first, and it is mostly a habit of waiting.

The reason is simple. On the day I finish a draft, I am the worst reader it will ever have. I know what every sentence was supposed to say, so when I read it over, I see what I meant instead of what is on the page. A paragraph that skips a step looks complete to me, because my mind quietly fills in the step. A joke that falls flat still makes me smile, because I remember why I thought it was funny.

Three days later I have forgotten just enough. The sentences have to do their own work now; I am no longer standing behind them, explaining. I find the paragraph that skips a step and the word I used four times on one page. Sometimes I find that the best sentence in the piece is in the last paragraph, where I finally worked out what I was trying to say, and that the whole thing should begin there.

People who hear about the drawer usually object that they do not have three days. Often that is true. A school assignment is due tomorrow; a letter needs an answer this week. But the drawer works in smaller sizes, too. Even a single night helps, and so does a walk around the block. What matters is that, for a while, the writer stops being the writer and comes back as a reader.

I have come to think the same is true of things that are spoken rather than written. The reply I want to give at once, in the heat of a disagreement, is the reply that makes sense to me, because I know everything I am feeling. A short wait lets me hear it the way the other person will.

Waiting can feel like idleness, and in a busy week it can seem like a luxury. I think it is closer to a tool, one of the few that costs nothing to use. The draft stays the same in the drawer. The reader who takes it out is the one who changes.

item.passage:
When I finish writing something, an essay or a long letter or a report for work, I put it in a drawer. Sometimes the drawer is real, and sometimes it is only a folder on my computer that I promise myself to leave closed. Either way, the piece stays there for at least three days before I read it again. Of everything I have learned about writing, this is the habit I would pass on first, and it is mostly a habit of waiting.

The reason is simple. On the day I finish a draft, I am the worst reader it will ever have. I know what every sentence was supposed to say, so when I read it over, I see what I meant instead of what is on the page. A paragraph that skips a step looks complete to me, because my mind quietly fills in the step. A joke that falls flat still makes me smile, because I remember why I thought it was funny.

Three days later I have forgotten just enough. The sentences have to do their own work now; I am no longer standing behind them, explaining. I find the paragraph that skips a step and the word I used four times on one page. Sometimes I find that the best sentence in the piece is in the last paragraph, where I finally worked out what I was trying to say, and that the whole thing should begin there.

People who hear about the drawer usually object that they do not have three days. Often that is true. A school assignment is due tomorrow; a letter needs an answer this week. But the drawer works in smaller sizes, too. Even a single night helps, and so does a walk around the block. What matters is that, for a while, the writer stops being the writer and comes back as a reader.

I have come to think the same is true of things that are spoken rather than written. The reply I want to give at once, in the heat of a disagreement, is the reply that makes sense to me, because I know everything I am feeling. A short wait lets me hear it the way the other person will.

Waiting can feel like idleness, and in a busy week it can seem like a luxury. I think it is closer to a tool, one of the few that costs nothing to use. The draft stays the same in the drawer. The reader who takes it out is the one who changes.

In 1884 the town of Tull's Crossing, a railroad stop of about twelve hundred people, had a bank, two churches, and a grain elevator, but no library. Books in town belonged to whoever had bought them, and most families owned only a handful. That spring a schoolteacher named Clara Wendt asked in the weekly paper for donations, and by June she had collected 212 volumes, from almanacs and books of sermons to a battered set of Dickens.

The books needed a home and a set of rules, and the second proved harder to settle than the first. A committee of six took a room above Harlan's dry-goods store, rent free, and built shelves along its walls. Then it argued for two evenings about whether books should leave the room, and for a third about whether to shelve novels at all. On the first question the majority said they should not. The collection was small, it had been given in trust, and a book carried off to a farm ten miles out might be gone for good. The room would be a reading room, open on Saturday afternoons and Wednesday evenings.

Wendt kept a count that first summer. On an average Saturday, she wrote, seven people climbed the stairs, and nearly all of them lived within a few blocks of the store. Farm families, who made up most of the district, came to town on Saturdays to sell and buy and seldom had an hour to spare for sitting and reading.

In October she brought the committee a proposal and a ledger. Any household could borrow two books at a time for three weeks. The borrower would sign the ledger beside the title, and a book returned late would cost a cent a day. The committee agreed to try lending for one winter, with two members voting against.

The ledger survives. Between November and March it records 940 loans, and the names in it include families from every road in the district. The most borrowed books were not the novels the committee had argued over but a veterinary manual and a guide to keeping farm accounts, each lent about as often as the three-week limit allowed. Nine books were lost that winter, most of them to wear rather than theft; beside one title Wendt wrote, "returned in two pieces, with apologies."

In the spring the committee voted to keep lending, and in 1891 the town meeting agreed to a small tax to buy new books each year. The room above Harlan's served until 1903, when the library moved into a brick building of its own. Wendt's first ledger went with it, to a shelf behind the front desk.

Walk through a lowland forest in Central or South America and you may see a moving line of green: hundreds of ants, each carrying a piece of leaf above its head like a small sail. These are leafcutter ants, and the leaves are not their food. The ants carry them underground to feed something else, a fungus that they grow in chambers inside the nest. The fungus is what the colony eats.

The arrangement is remarkably complete. Medium-sized workers cut fresh pieces of leaf and carry them home, sometimes from trees a long way from the nest. Inside, smaller workers cut the pieces into still smaller bits, chew them into a pulp, and press the pulp into a spongy garden. The fungus spreads through this garden and produces tiny swollen tips, rich in nutrients, which the ants harvest and feed to their young. The adults appear to take some food from the fungus as well, along with plant sap they drink while cutting.

The work is divided largely by size. In a big colony, workers range from tiny ants that tend the fungus to large-headed soldiers many times their size that defend the nest. Some of the smallest workers ride out to the cutting sites and back on the leaf pieces themselves. Researchers who have studied these riders suggest that they help guard the carriers against small parasitic flies that try to lay eggs in the ants.

Like any farmer, the ants must deal with pests. A mold that attacks the fungus can ruin a garden. Many leafcutter ants carry bacteria on their bodies that produce substances which seem to slow this mold, and workers also remove infected pieces of garden and carry them away from the garden to separate waste sites. Biologists still debate how much each of these defenses contributes.

The fungus that leafcutters grow is not known to live anywhere outside their nests; it appears to depend on the ants as completely as they depend on it. When a young queen leaves to start a new colony, she carries a small pellet of the fungus in a pouch in her mouth. After mating, she digs a chamber, spits out the pellet, and tends the first garden herself.

A mature colony can hold millions of workers and strip a remarkable amount of plant material in a year. For this reason leafcutters are sometimes counted as pests on farms. They are also, by some estimates, among the most important plant-eaters in the forests where they live, although the leaves they cut feed their fungus rather than themselves.
